claim: Marfan syndrome is a systemic connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in FBN1, the gene encoding extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1.
source: Marfan syndrome is a systemic connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in FBN1, the gene encoding extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome.

claim: A major cause of mortality in Marfan patients is aortic dissection and rupture.
source: A major cause of mortality in Marfan patients is aortic dissection and rupture.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about Marfan syndrome complications.

claim: In Marfan mice, multiple phenotypic manifestations, including aortic aneurysm, developmental lung emphysema, mitral valve disease, and skeletal muscle myopathy, correlate with enhanced transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signaling.
source: In Marfan mice, multiple phenotypic manifestations, including aortic aneurysm, developmental lung emphysema, mitral valve disease, and skeletal muscle myopathy, correlate with enhanced transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signaling, while treatment with either TGFβ neutralizing antibody (NAb) or the angiotensin-II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blocker (ARB) losartan can ameliorate these phenotypes, in association with evidence of reduced TGFβ signaling (Neptune et al., 2003; Ng et al., 2004; Habashi et al., 2006; Cohn et al., 2007; Cook et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Treatment with either TGFβ neutralizing antibody (NAb) or the angiotensin-II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blocker (ARB) losartan can ameliorate phenotypes in Marfan mice, in association with evidence of reduced TGFβ signaling.
source: In Marfan mice, multiple phenotypic manifestations, including aortic aneurysm, developmental lung emphysema, mitral valve disease, and skeletal muscle myopathy, correlate with enhanced transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signaling, while treatment with either TGFβ neutralizing antibody (NAb) or the angiotensin-II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blocker (ARB) losartan can ameliorate these phenotypes, in association with evidence of reduced TGFβ signaling (Neptune et al., 2003; Ng et al., 2004; Habashi et al., 2006; Cohn et al., 2007; Cook et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Both canonical (Smad2/3) and noncanonical (ERK1/2) TGFβ-dependent signaling cascades have been shown to be activated in the aortas of Marfan mice.
source: Both canonical (Smad2/3) and noncanonical (ERK1/2) TGFβ-dependent signaling cascades have been shown to be activated in the aortas of Marfan mice, while selective inhibition of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) activation using RDEA119 (refametinib) rescues aortic growth and aortic wall architecture in Marfan mice (Habashi et al., 2011; Holm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Selective inhibition of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) activation using RDEA119 (refametinib) rescues aortic growth and aortic wall architecture in Marfan mice.
source: Both canonical (Smad2/3) and noncanonical (ERK1/2) TGFβ-dependent signaling cascades have been shown to be activated in the aortas of Marfan mice, while selective inhibition of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) activation using RDEA119 (refametinib) rescues aortic growth and aortic wall architecture in Marfan mice (Habashi et al., 2011; Holm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are a class of blood pressure lowering medications that block movement of calcium into cells from the extracellular space.
source: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are a class of blood pressure lowering medications that block movement of calcium into cells from the extracellular space.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about the mechanism of action of CCBs.

claim: There are several sub-classes of CCB based on chemical structure, including dihydropyridines (e.g., amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines, which include both phenylalkylamines (e.g., verapamil) and benzothiazepines (e.g., diltiazem).
source: There are several sub-classes of CCB based on chemical structure, including dihydropyridines (e.g., amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines, which include both phenylalkylamines (e.g., verapamil) and benzothiazepines (e.g., diltiazem).
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about CCB classification.

claim: CCBs are currently considered an alternative therapeutic strategy for Marfan patients intolerant of β-blockers, due to their ability to reduce contractility of the heart (negative ionotropy) and to lower blood pressure.
source: CCBs are currently considered an alternative therapeutic strategy for Marfan patients intolerant of β-blockers, due to their ability to reduce contractility of the heart (negative ionotropy) and to lower blood pressure (Milewicz et al., 2005; von Kodolitsch and Robinson, 2007; Hartog et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: There is limited empirical evidence for the safety or utility of CCBs in patients with Marfan syndrome and other forms of inherited thoracic aortic aneurysm.
source: However, there is limited empirical evidence for their safety or utility in patients with Marfan syndrome and other forms of inherited thoracic aortic aneurysm (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: The Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model is heterozygous for a cysteine substitution in an epidermal growth factor-like domain in fibrillin-1, representative of the most common class of mutations causing Marfan syndrome.
source: To address this, we assessed the effect of two major classes of CCB in a mouse line heterozygous for a cysteine substitution in an epidermal growth factor-like domain in fibrillin-1 (Fbn1C1039G/+), representative of the most common class of mutations causing Marfan syndrome.
evidence: This is a description of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: The Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model has been shown previously to closely recapitulate many of the phenotypic manifestations seen in patients with Marfan syndrome, including aortic aneurysm.
source: This mouse model has been shown previously to closely recapitulate many of the phenotypic manifestations seen in patients with the disorder, including aortic aneurysm (Habashi et al., 2006; Holm et al., 2011; Cook et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Amlodipine at 12 mg/kg/day resulted in a similar reduction in blood pressure as is obtained using losartan in the Marfan mouse model.
source: They were treated with a dose of amlodipine (12 mg/kg/day) that resulted in a similar reduction in blood pressure as is obtained using losartan in our Marfan mouse model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S1.

claim: Between 2 and 4 months of age, placebo-treated Marfan mice showed greater aortic root growth than WT littermates.
source: Between 2 and 4 months of age, placebo-treated Marfan mice showed greater aortic root growth than WT littermates, which was unexpectedly exacerbated by amlodipine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Aortic root growth in Marfan mice was unexpectedly exacerbated by amlodipine.
source: Between 2 and 4 months of age, placebo-treated Marfan mice showed greater aortic root growth than WT littermates, which was unexpectedly exacerbated by amlodipine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Amlodipine exacerbation of aortic root growth was seen in both WT and Marfan mice but was of greater magnitude in the Marfan animals, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the mice.
source: This exacerbation was seen in both WT and Marfan mice but was of greater magnitude in the Marfan animals, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the mice (genotype effect: p < 0.0001, amlodipine effect: p < 0.001, interaction effect: p < 0.01, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Amlodipine-treated WT and Marfan mice showed striking dilatation of the ascending aorta.
source: Amlodipine-treated WT and Marfan mice also showed striking dilatation of the ascending aorta, an aortic segment just distal to the aortic root, which is less commonly affected in people and mice with Marfan syndrome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The ascending aorta is less commonly affected in people and mice with Marfan syndrome.
source: Amlodipine-treated WT and Marfan mice also showed striking dilatation of the ascending aorta, an aortic segment just distal to the aortic root, which is less commonly affected in people and mice with Marfan syndrome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the typical pattern of aortic involvement in Marfan syndrome.

claim: Amlodipine-induced growth in the ascending aorta was several fold greater than that seen in the aortic root, with Marfan mice appearing particularly susceptible.
source: Amlodipine-induced growth in the ascending aorta was several fold greater than that seen in the aortic root, with Marfan mice again appearing particularly susceptible (genotype effect: p < 0.0001, amlodipine effect: p < 0.0001, interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No WT or placebo-treated Marfan mice died during the 3-month drug trial.
source: Furthermore, while no WT or placebo-treated Marfan mice died during the 3-month drug trial, more than 40% of amlodipine-treated Marfan mice died secondary to aortic rupture, as evidenced by hemothorax or hemopericardium (p < 0.01, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: More than 40% of amlodipine-treated Marfan mice died secondary to aortic rupture, as evidenced by hemothorax or hemopericardium.
source: Furthermore, while no WT or placebo-treated Marfan mice died during the 3-month drug trial, more than 40% of amlodipine-treated Marfan mice died secondary to aortic rupture, as evidenced by hemothorax or hemopericardium (p < 0.01, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data and pathological findings shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Latex injection of the vasculature illustrated the enlargement of the ascending aorta in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice.
source: Following death or sacrifice, latex injection of the vasculature illustrated the enlargement of the ascending aorta in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S2.

claim: Histologic analyses revealed greater ascending aortic wall thickening, elastic fiber fragmentation, reduced elastin content, and increased collagen deposition in Marfan animals compared to WT littermates, all of which were exacerbated by amlodipine treatment.
source: Histologic analyses revealed greater ascending aortic wall thickening, elastic fiber fragmentation, reduced elastin content, and increased collagen deposition in Marfan animals compared to WT littermates, all of which were exacerbated by amlodipine treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Amlodipine had no effect on aortic architecture in WT animals.
source: While amlodipine had no effect on aortic architecture in WT animals (p = 0.16), it induced significant histological damage in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.001, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative histological scoring data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Amlodipine induced significant histological damage in Marfan mice.
source: While amlodipine had no effect on aortic architecture in WT animals (p = 0.16), it induced significant histological damage in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.001, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative histological scoring data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The deleterious histological effects of amlodipine were not observed in the descending thoracic aorta of Marfan mice.
source: Interestingly, these deleterious histological effects of amlodipine were not observed in the descending thoracic aorta of Marfan mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S3; p = 0.86, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S4), an aortic segment that lacks predisposition for dilatation or evidence of increased TGFβ signaling in Marfan mice (Haskett et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S3 and 1S4.

claim: The descending thoracic aorta is an aortic segment that lacks predisposition for dilatation or evidence of increased TGFβ signaling in Marfan mice.
source: Interestingly, these deleterious histological effects of amlodipine were not observed in the descending thoracic aorta of Marfan mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S3; p = 0.86, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S4), an aortic segment that lacks predisposition for dilatation or evidence of increased TGFβ signaling in Marfan mice (Haskett et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: Prior studies assessing the effects of CCBs in other mouse models of aortic disease, such as the angiotensin-II infusion model, have typically used lower doses of amlodipine, in the range of 1 to 5 mg/kg/day.
source: Prior studies assessing the effects of CCBs in other mouse models of aortic disease, such as the angiotensin-II infusion model, have typically used lower doses of amlodipine, in the range of 1 to 5 mg/kg/day (Chen et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Even at a dose of 3 mg/kg/day, amlodipine still exacerbated both aortic root and ascending aortic growth in WT mice and Marfan littermates, with greater accentuation occurring in the ascending aorta and in Marfan animals.
source: Even at this lower dose, amlodipine still exacerbated both aortic root and ascending aortic growth in WT mice and Marfan littermates, with greater accentuation again occurring in the ascending aorta and in Marfan animals (aortic root interaction effect: p < 0.01, ascending aorta interaction effect: p < 0.01, Figure 1—figure supplement 1S5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S5.

claim: Compared to placebo-treated WT and Marfan mice, verapamil-treated animals showed enhanced growth in both the aortic root and ascending aorta, with greater accentuation occurring in Marfan animals, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the mice.
source: Compared to placebo-treated WT and Marfan mice, verapamil-treated animals showed enhanced growth in both the aortic root and ascending aorta, with greater accentuation again occurring in Marfan animals, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the mice (aortic root interaction effect: p < 0.01, ascending aorta interaction effect: p < 0.01, Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1S1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1S1.

claim: Verapamil had no effect on aortic architecture in WT mice.
source: While verapamil had no effect on aortic architecture in WT mice, it significantly exacerbated the histological changes seen in the ascending aortic wall of Marfan mice, both qualitatively (Figure 2B) and quantitatively (interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Verapamil significantly exacerbated the histological changes seen in the ascending aortic wall of Marfan mice.
source: While verapamil had no effect on aortic architecture in WT mice, it significantly exacerbated the histological changes seen in the ascending aortic wall of Marfan mice, both qualitatively (Figure 2B) and quantitatively (interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Verapamil had no effect on aortic architecture in the descending thoracic aorta of Marfan mice.
source: As with amlodipine, verapamil had no effect on aortic architecture in the descending thoracic aorta of Marfan mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1S2; p = 0.72, Figure 2—figure supplement 1S3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1S2 and 1S3.

claim: Treatment with amlodipine accentuated signaling changes previously observed in Marfan mice, including enhanced activation of both canonical (Smad) and noncanonical (ERK1/2) TGFβ-dependent signaling cascades.
source: Treatment with amlodipine accentuated signaling changes previously observed in Marfan mice, including enhanced activation of both canonical (Smad) and noncanonical (ERK1/2) TGFβ-dependent signaling cascades, when normalized to either β-Actin or their respective total proteins (Smad3 treatment effect: p < 0.0001, ERK1/2 treatment effect: p < 0.01, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Amlodipine had a greater effect on Smad3 and ERK1/2 activation in Marfan mice than WT littermates, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the animals.
source: Again, amlodipine had a greater effect in Marfan mice than WT littermates, indicating a specific interaction between the drug and the genotype of the animals (Smad3 interaction effect: p < 0.001, ERK1/2 interaction effect: p < 0.01, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Combined treatment with amlodipine and the selective inhibitor of ERK1/2 activation RDEA119 prevented amlodipine-induced ascending aortic enlargement.
source: Combined treatment with amlodipine and the selective inhibitor of ERK1/2 activation RDEA119 prevented amlodipine-induced ascending aortic enlargement (treatment effect: p < 0.0001), with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.001, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RDEA119 rescued the premature lethality seen in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice.
source: Furthermore, RDEA119 rescued the premature lethality (p < 0.05, Figure 3C), and alterations in aortic wall architecture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1S1; interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1S2), seen in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice, in association with abrogated ERK1/2 activation (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RDEA119 rescued alterations in aortic wall architecture seen in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice, in association with abrogated ERK1/2 activation.
source: Furthermore, RDEA119 rescued the premature lethality (p < 0.05, Figure 3C), and alterations in aortic wall architecture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1S1; interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1S2), seen in amlodipine-treated Marfan mice, in association with abrogated ERK1/2 activation (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1S1, 1S2, and Figure 3D.

claim: RDEA119 had no significant effect on Smad3 activation.
source: RDEA119 had no significant effect on Smad3 activation (p = 0.26, Figure 3D), suggesting that rescue of CCB-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice can occur independent of Smad3 activation status.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Rescue of CCB-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice can occur independent of Smad3 activation status.
source: RDEA119 had no significant effect on Smad3 activation (p = 0.26, Figure 3D), suggesting that rescue of CCB-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice can occur independent of Smad3 activation status.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RDEA119 rescues the phenotype without affecting Smad3 activation.

claim: Enhanced ERK1/2 activation is a critical mediator of CCB-mediated aortic aneurysm progression in Marfan mice.
source: In contrast, these data suggest that enhanced ERK1/2 activation is a critical mediator of CCB-mediated aortic aneurysm progression in Marfan mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ERK1/2 inhibition rescues the CCB-induced phenotype.

claim: ERK1/2 activation in Marfan mice has been shown to be AT1R dependent, since the AT1R blocker (ARB) losartan can rescue aortic root growth in Marfan animals in association with normalization of ERK1/2 activation.
source: ERK1/2 activation in Marfan mice has previously been shown to also be AT1R dependent, since the AT1R blocker (ARB) losartan can rescue aortic root growth in Marfan animals in association with normalization of ERK1/2 activation (Holm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: Losartan prevented amlodipine-induced ascending aortic aneurysm growth, with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice.
source: Losartan also prevented amlodipine-induced ascending aortic aneurysm growth (treatment effect: p < 0.01), with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.001, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Losartan prevention of amlodipine-induced ascending aortic aneurysm growth correlated with reduced ERK1/2 activation.
source: This correlated with reduced ERK1/2 activation in these animals (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The deleterious effect of CCBs in Marfan mice is AT1R-dependent.
source: Hence the deleterious effect of CCBs in Marfan mice also appears to be AT1R-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that losartan (an AT1R blocker) prevents the CCB-induced phenotype.

claim: TGFβ-dependent gene expression can be mediated by protein kinase C (PKC) in both human fibroblasts and aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs).
source: There is evidence that TGFβ-dependent gene expression can be mediated by protein kinase C (PKC) in both human fibroblasts and aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) (Mulsow et al., 2005; Ryer et al., 2006), and PKC blockade can inhibit TGFβ-dependent phenotypes and gene expression in vitro and in vivo (Li and Jimenez, 2011; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: PKC blockade can inhibit TGFβ-dependent phenotypes and gene expression in vitro and in vivo.
source: There is evidence that TGFβ-dependent gene expression can be mediated by protein kinase C (PKC) in both human fibroblasts and aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) (Mulsow et al., 2005; Ryer et al., 2006), and PKC blockade can inhibit TGFβ-dependent phenotypes and gene expression in vitro and in vivo (Li and Jimenez, 2011; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Angiotensin-II has been shown to activate ERK1/2 via PKC.
source: Furthermore, angiotensin-II has been shown to activate ERK1/2 via PKC (Shah and Catt, 2002; Olivares Reyes et al., 2005; Olson et al., 2008), with TGFβ potentially serving as an intermediary in this process (Uchiyama-Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: TGFβ potentially serves as an intermediary in the process of angiotensin-II activating ERK1/2 via PKC.
source: Furthermore, angiotensin-II has been shown to activate ERK1/2 via PKC (Shah and Catt, 2002; Olivares Reyes et al., 2005; Olson et al., 2008), with TGFβ potentially serving as an intermediary in this process (Uchiyama-Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: PKCβ activation was significantly greater in Marfan mice than WT littermates.
source: Western blot analysis of the aortic root and ascending aorta showed that PKCβ activation was significantly greater in Marfan mice than WT littermates (genotype effect: p < 0.0001), and both TGFβ NAb and losartan significantly reduced it (treatment effect: p < 0.0001 for both, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Both TGFβ NAb and losartan significantly reduced PKCβ activation in Marfan mice.
source: Western blot analysis of the aortic root and ascending aorta showed that PKCβ activation was significantly greater in Marfan mice than WT littermates (genotype effect: p < 0.0001), and both TGFβ NAb and losartan significantly reduced it (treatment effect: p < 0.0001 for both, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The effects of TGFβ NAb and losartan on PKCβ activation closely paralleled their effects on ERK1/2 activation.
source: This closely paralleled their effects on ERK1/2 activation (Figures 3F, 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 3F and 4A.

claim: Amlodipine treatment accentuated PKCβ activation in Marfan mice, in association with increased activation of phospholipase C (PLCγ), its upstream activator, both of which were rescued by treatment with losartan.
source: Furthermore, amlodipine treatment accentuated PKCβ activation in Marfan mice, in association with increased activation of phospholipase C (PLCγ), its upstream activator, both of which were rescued by treatment with losartan (treatment effect: p < 0.0001 for both, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PKCβ and its upstream activator PLCγ are both TGFβ- and AT1R-dependent in Marfan mice.
source: These data suggest that PKCβ and its upstream activator PLCγ are both TGFβ- and AT1R-dependent in Marfan mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TGFβ NAb and losartan (AT1R blocker) both reduce PKCβ and PLCγ activation.

claim: Enzastaurin is a PKC inhibitor with relative selectivity for PKCβ and has been shown previously to inhibit PKC-mediated ERK1/2 activation.
source: Enzastaurin is a PKC inhibitor with relative selectivity for PKCβ and has been shown previously to inhibit PKC-mediated ERK1/2 activation (Ruvolo et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Enzastaurin competes with ATP for the nucleotide triphosphate-binding site of PKC, thereby blocking its activation.
source: It competes with ATP for the nucleotide triphosphate-binding site of PKC, thereby blocking its activation (Graff et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: Treatment with enzastaurin led to a significant reduction in ascending aortic growth in amlodipine-treated animals, with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice.
source: In keeping with the hypothesis that PKCβ mediates CCB-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice, treatment with enzastaurin led to a significant reduction in ascending aortic growth in amlodipine-treated animals (treatment effect: p < 0.0001), with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Enzastaurin significantly rescued the deleterious histological changes imposed on the Marfan aorta by amlodipine.
source: Enzastaurin also significantly rescued the deleterious histological changes imposed on the Marfan aorta by amlodipine, both qualitatively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1S2) and quantitatively (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1S3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1S2 and 1S3.

claim: PKCβ mediates amlodipine-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice.
source: Cumulatively, these data suggest that PKCβ mediates amlodipine-induced aortic aneurysm exacerbation in Marfan mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PKCβ inhibition with enzastaurin prevents the amlodipine-induced phenotype.

claim: Enzastaurin was able to significantly reduce aortic root growth in both WT and Marfan mice.
source: This showed that enzastaurin was indeed able to significantly reduce aortic root growth in both WT and Marfan mice (treatment effect: p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The protection conferred on aortic growth by enzastaurin correlated with a significant reduction in PKCβ activation in both placebo- and amlodipine-treated Marfan mice.
source: Western blot analysis of the aortic root and ascending aorta confirmed that the protection conferred on aortic growth by enzastaurin correlated with a significant reduction in PKCβ activation in both placebo- and amlodipine-treated Marfan mice (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Enzastaurin was able to significantly rescue ERK1/2 activation in Marfan mice.
source: Furthermore, enzastaurin was able to significantly rescue ERK1/2 activation in these animals (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 4E), inferring that PKCβ may mediate ERK1/2 activation in this setting.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PKCβ may mediate ERK1/2 activation in Marfan mice.
source: Furthermore, enzastaurin was able to significantly rescue ERK1/2 activation in these animals (treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 4E), inferring that PKCβ may mediate ERK1/2 activation in this setting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PKCβ inhibition with enzastaurin reduces ERK1/2 activation.

claim: Hydralazine has been shown to inhibit PKC-mediated ERK1/2 activation in vivo.
source: We became interested in the clinically available antihypertensive agent hydralazine, not only because it reduces blood pressure (a desirable effect in Marfan syndrome) but also because it has been shown to inhibit PKC-mediated ERK1/2 activation in vivo (Deng et al., 2003; Gorelik et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: Hydralazine at a dose of 16 mg/kg/day reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure by roughly 10–15% in mice.
source: This dose of hydralazine reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure by roughly 10–15% in our mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1S1).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood pressure data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S1.

claim: Compared to WT mice, placebo-treated Marfan animals showed greater aortic root growth, which was fully rescued by hydralazine.
source: Compared to WT mice, placebo-treated Marfan animals showed greater aortic root growth, which was fully rescued by hydralazine (genotype effect: p < 0.001, treatment effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hydralazine treatment led to a significant rescue of aortic wall architecture, with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice.
source: Hydralazine treatment also led to a significant rescue of aortic wall architecture, with the magnitude of effect being significantly greater in Marfan mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1S3; interaction effect: p < 0.001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1S4).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S3 and 1S4.

claim: Hydralazine rescue of aortic wall architecture correlated with a reduction of both PKCβ and ERK1/2 activation in the aortas of Marfan mice.
source: This correlated with a reduction of both PKCβ and ERK1/2 activation in the aortas of these animals (treatment effect: p < 0.0001 for both, Figure 5B), with the magnitude of effect again being greater in Marfan mice (interaction effect: p < 0.001 and p < 0.0001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PKCβ activation was greater in the aortas of Marfan mice compared to WT littermates.
source: While PKCβ activation was greater in the aortas of Marfan mice compared to WT littermates (genotype effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5), and this was exacerbated by amlodipine (treatment effect: p < 0.0001), RDEA119 had no significant effect on PKCβ activation (post-hoc analysis: p = 0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5.

claim: PKCβ activation was exacerbated by amlodipine in Marfan mice.
source: While PKCβ activation was greater in the aortas of Marfan mice compared to WT littermates (genotype effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5), and this was exacerbated by amlodipine (treatment effect: p < 0.0001), RDEA119 had no significant effect on PKCβ activation (post-hoc analysis: p = 0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5.

claim: RDEA119 had no significant effect on PKCβ activation.
source: While PKCβ activation was greater in the aortas of Marfan mice compared to WT littermates (genotype effect: p < 0.0001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5), and this was exacerbated by amlodipine (treatment effect: p < 0.0001), RDEA119 had no significant effect on PKCβ activation (post-hoc analysis: p = 0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1S5.

claim: PKCβ lies upstream of ERK1/2 in the pathogenic sequence of events driving aortic aneurysm progression in Marfan mice.
source: This suggests that PKCβ lies upstream of ERK1/2 in the pathogenic sequence of events driving aortic aneurysm progression in Marfan mice and suggests that both enzastaurin and hydralazine achieve their beneficial effect in Marfan animals via inhibition of PKCβ-mediated ERK1/2 activation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ERK1/2 inhibition does not affect PKCβ activation, suggesting PKCβ is upstream.

claim: Both enzastaurin and hydralazine achieve their beneficial effect in Marfan animals via inhibition of PKCβ-mediated ERK1/2 activation.
source: This suggests that PKCβ lies upstream of ERK1/2 in the pathogenic sequence of events driving aortic aneurysm progression in Marfan mice and suggests that both enzastaurin and hydralazine achieve their beneficial effect in Marfan animals via inhibition of PKCβ-mediated ERK1/2 activation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both drugs reduce PKCβ and ERK1/2 activation and rescue the phenotype.

claim: Marfan patients with native aortic roots at the time of enrollment who received CCBs (as compared to other antihypertensive agents) had an increased odds of aortic dissection (odds ratio 12.5, p = 0.032).
source: Marfan patients with native aortic roots at the time of enrollment (n = 531) who received CCBs (as compared to other antihypertensive agents) had an increased odds of aortic dissection (odds ratio (OR) 12.5, p = 0.032).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data from the GenTAC registry.

claim: CCB-treated Marfan patients had an increased odds of needing aortic surgery (OR 5.5, p < 0.001) when compared to patients on other antihypertensive agents.
source: In keeping with this hypothesis, we found that CCB-treated Marfan patients had an increased odds of needing aortic surgery (OR 5.5, p < 0.001) when compared to patients on other antihypertensive agents, which remained significant when corrected for either blood pressure (OR 5.4, p < 0.001) or aortic size (OR 5.0, p < 0.01) at enrollment.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data from the GenTAC registry.

claim: For patients with other forms of iTAA and native aortic roots at the time of enrollment, CCB-treated patients had an increased odds of needing aortic surgery (OR 2.4, p = 0.004).
source: For patients with other forms of iTAA and native aortic roots at the time of enrollment (n = 1819), there was suggestion of an increased odds for aortic dissection in those who had taken CCBs, although this did not reach statistical significance (OR 4.7, p = 0.26). This was again most likely secondary to prophylactic surgical intervention, given that CCB-treated patients did have an increased odds of needing aortic surgery (OR 2.4, p = 0.004), which remained significant when corrected for either blood pressure (OR 2.2, p = 0.016) or aortic size (OR 2.2, p = 0.017) at enrollment.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data from the GenTAC registry.

claim: The odds of aortic dissection and aortic surgery remained significantly increased in Marfan patients on CCBs after controlling for β-blocker use (OR 15.9, p = 0.045; OR 5.7, p < 0.01; respectively).
source: To further assess this, we controlled for β-blocker use in our GenTAC analysis (Table 1) and found that it did not fundamentally alter the conclusions of the study. The odds of aortic dissection and aortic surgery remained significantly increased in Marfan patients on CCBs (OR 15.9, p = 0.045; OR 5.7, p < 0.01; respectively), while the odds of aortic surgery remained significantly increased in other iTAA syndrome patients on CCBs (OR 2.0, p = 0.026).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data from the GenTAC registry after controlling for β-blocker use.

claim: The odds of aortic surgery remained significantly increased in other iTAA syndrome patients on CCBs after controlling for β-blocker use (OR 2.0, p = 0.026).
source: To further assess this, we controlled for β-blocker use in our GenTAC analysis (Table 1) and found that it did not fundamentally alter the conclusions of the study. The odds of aortic dissection and aortic surgery remained significantly increased in Marfan patients on CCBs (OR 15.9, p = 0.045; OR 5.7, p < 0.01; respectively), while the odds of aortic surgery remained significantly increased in other iTAA syndrome patients on CCBs (OR 2.0, p = 0.026).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of clinical data from the GenTAC registry after controlling for β-blocker use.

claim: Prior studies in mouse models of Marfan syndrome and related disorders have shown that β-blockers (e.g., propranolol) or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi, e.g., enalapril) achieve a relatively modest inhibition of aortic aneurysm growth and fail to preserve aortic wall architecture when compared to the ARB losartan, despite an equivalent reduction in blood pressure.
source: Prior studies in mouse models of Marfan syndrome and related disorders have shown that β-blockers (e.g., propranolol) (Habashi et al., 2006; Gallo et al., 2014) or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi, e.g., enalapril) (Habashi et al., 2011) achieve a relatively modest inhibition of aortic aneurysm growth and fail to preserve aortic wall architecture when compared to the ARB losartan, despite an equivalent reduction in blood pressure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: In Marfan mice the extent of relative protection of different antihypertensive agents correlates closely with suppression of TGFβ-dependent canonical (Smad2/3) or noncanonical (ERK1/2) signaling.
source: Notably, in Marfan mice the extent of relative protection of these agents correlates closely with suppression of TGFβ-dependent canonical (Smad2/3) or noncanonical (ERK1/2) signaling (Holm et al., 2011; Cook et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: This is the first time that a class of clinically available blood pressure lowering agents has been shown to exacerbate aortic aneurysm and cause dissection in a mouse model of Marfan syndrome.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time that a class of clinically available blood pressure lowering agents has been shown to exacerbate aortic aneurysm and cause dissection in a mouse model of Marfan syndrome.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Amlodipine lowered blood pressure equally as much as losartan.
source: This is despite the fact that amlodipine lowered blood pressure equally as much as losartan, an effect which should provide some degree of protection against aneurysm progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Verapamil is generally considered to have greater selectivity for cardiac tissue, while amlodipine is considered to have stronger tropism for aortic VSMCs.
source: While the two drugs both target L-type calcium channels on the cell membrane, verapamil is generally considered to have greater selectivity for cardiac tissue, while amlodipine is considered to have stronger tropism for aortic VSMCs.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about the tissue selectivity of these drugs.

claim: Amlodipine has a relatively greater detrimental effect on the aorta compared to verapamil, possibly due to its stronger tropism for aortic VSMCs.
source: It may be for this reason that amlodipine has a relatively greater detrimental effect on the aorta compared to verapamil.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in effects between the two drugs and their known tissue selectivity.

claim: ARBs such as losartan and ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are teratogenic and hence not appropriate for use in pregnancy.
source: While ARBs such as losartan and ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are teratogenic and hence not appropriate for use in pregnancy, hydralazine is well tolerated, making it an appealing alternative therapeutic strategy for Marfan syndrome, particularly in pregnant women.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the teratogenicity of these drug classes.

claim: Hydralazine is well tolerated, making it an appealing alternative therapeutic strategy for Marfan syndrome, particularly in pregnant women.
source: While ARBs such as losartan and ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are teratogenic and hence not appropriate for use in pregnancy, hydralazine is well tolerated, making it an appealing alternative therapeutic strategy for Marfan syndrome, particularly in pregnant women.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing hydralazine's efficacy and established knowledge about its safety profile.

claim: CCBs have an even more pronounced effect on the more distal ascending aorta compared to the aortic root, an aortic segment that is less frequently affected in Marfan syndrome.
source: It is also notable that while CCBs accelerate growth of the aortic root in Marfan mice, they have an even more pronounced effect on the more distal ascending aorta, an aortic segment that is less frequently affected in Marfan syndrome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Vascular smooth muscle cells in the aortic root primarily derive from the second heart field (SHF), while those in the more distal ascending aorta derive from the cardiac neural crest (CNC).
source: While vascular smooth muscle cells in the aortic root primarily derive from the second heart field (SHF), those in the more distal ascending aorta derive from the cardiac neural crest (CNC).
evidence: This is established developmental biology knowledge about the embryonic origins of vascular smooth muscle cells.

claim: L-type calcium channel function is critical for correct CNC migration, differentiation, and morphogenic patterning, as well as maintenance of an appropriate post-developmental differentiated state.
source: Prior work has shown that L-type calcium channel function is critical for correct CNC migration, differentiation, and morphogenic patterning, as well as maintenance of an appropriate post-developmental differentiated state (Moran, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: Mutations in L-type calcium channels result in cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia in neural-crest-derived tissues.
source: Furthermore, mutations in L-type calcium channels result in cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia in neural-crest-derived tissues (Ramachandran et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published research.

claim: CCBs appear to have a greater deleterious effect on the ascending aorta compared to the aortic root, possibly due to the neural crest origin of ascending aortic smooth muscle cells.
source: This may explain why CCBs appear to have a greater deleterious effect on the ascending aorta compared to the aortic root.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed regional differences in CCB effects and knowledge about developmental origins and calcium channel function.

claim: The ascending aorta is characteristically involved in patients with BAV with aneurysm.
source: Interestingly, the ascending aorta is characteristically involved in patients with BAV with aneurysm.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the pattern of aortic involvement in BAV.

claim: BAV is the most common developmental cardiovascular abnormality in humans.
source: Despite being the most common developmental cardiovascular abnormality in humans, the genetic cause(s) and molecular mechanisms underlying BAV and the associated aortopathy are not well understood.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the prevalence of BAV.

claim: The genetic cause(s) and molecular mechanisms underlying BAV and the associated aortopathy are not well understood.
source: Despite being the most common developmental cardiovascular abnormality in humans, the genetic cause(s) and molecular mechanisms underlying BAV and the associated aortopathy are not well understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of understanding of BAV.

claim: This work provides rationale and incentive to elucidate whether altered calcium, PKC and/or ERK1/2 signaling may play a role in BAV with aneurysm.
source: This work provides rationale and incentive to elucidate whether altered calcium, PKC and/or ERK1/2 signaling may play a role in this condition.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions based on the findings of the study.

claim: There is only one prior study assessing the effect of CCBs on aortic growth in Marfan patients.
source: There is only one prior study assessing the effect of CCBs on aortic growth in Marfan patients (Rossi-Foulkes et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a claim about the literature based on the authors' knowledge and citation.

claim: In the prior study by Rossi-Foulkes et al., the number of CCB-treated patients was small (n = 6), and the study combined data on patients treated with either CCBs or β-blockers.
source: The number of CCB-treated patients was small (n = 6), and the study combined data on patients treated with either CCBs or β-blockers.
evidence: This is a description of the design of a prior study based on citation.

claim: β-blockers are known to confer protection against aortic growth in Marfan patients.
source: Given that β-blockers are known to confer protection against aortic growth in Marfan patients (Salim et al., 1994; Shores et al., 1994; Silverman et al., 1995), and nearly 80% of patients in the study were on β-blockers but not CCBs, a detrimental effect of CCBs could easily have been masked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research.

claim: In the Rossi-Foulkes et al. study, the complication rate was more than twice as high in CCB-treated patients as compared to those on β-blockers (33% vs 15%).
source: Interestingly in the study, the complication rate was more than twice as high in CCB-treated patients as compared to those on β-blockers (33% vs 15%), although numbers were too small to draw firm conclusions.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study based on citation.

claim: Randomized double-blinded prospective clinical trials are the preferred approach to analyze the therapeutic efficacy of a drug.
source: While randomized double-blinded prospective clinical trials are the preferred approach to analyze the therapeutic efficacy of a drug, this is not really feasible for agents that are found to be severely detrimental in pre-clinical models, since ethical approval for a prospective human trial is unlikely to be granted.
evidence: This is established knowledge about clinical trial methodology and ethics.

claim: Ethical approval for a prospective human trial is unlikely to be granted for agents that are found to be severely detrimental in pre-clinical models.
source: While randomized double-blinded prospective clinical trials are the preferred approach to analyze the therapeutic efficacy of a drug, this is not really feasible for agents that are found to be severely detrimental in pre-clinical models, since ethical approval for a prospective human trial is unlikely to be granted.
evidence: This is established knowledge about clinical trial ethics.

claim: Retrospective analyses of large data sets are a more realistic solution for assessing drugs found to be severely detrimental in pre-clinical models.
source: Retrospective analyses of large data sets are a more realistic solution in such scenarios.
evidence: This is an inference about appropriate research methodology given ethical constraints.

claim: The human data in this study is limited by relatively small sample size (more so for aortic dissection than aortic surgery) and an inability to control for the dose or number of medications that patients were receiving.
source: However, it needs to be recognized that the human data contained herein is still limited by relatively small sample size (more so for aortic dissection than aortic surgery) and an inability to control for the dose or number of medications that patients were receiving.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the clinical data analysis.

claim: Aortic size at the time of enrollment is an indicator of baseline aortic disease severity and a predictor of future risk of aortic dissection and/or need for aortic surgery.
source: We were able to control for aortic size at the time of enrollment, which is an indicator of baseline aortic disease severity and a predictor of future risk of aortic dissection and/or need for aortic surgery.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about risk factors for aortic complications.

claim: Blood pressure is a known risk factor for aneurysm progression.
source: We were also able to control for blood pressure, which is a known risk factor for aneurysm progression.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about risk factors for aneurysm progression.

claim: The data suggest that CCBs should be used with caution in Marfan patients.
source: Hence while the conclusions that can be drawn are not definitive, the data suggest that CCBs should be used with caution in Marfan patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined mouse and human data from the study.

claim: The data suggest that CCBs may be deleterious in other Marfan-related conditions.
source: They also suggest that CCBs may be deleterious in other Marfan-related conditions, although a larger sample size will be needed to assess risk after stratification by individual disorders.
evidence: This is an inference based on the human data from the study, with acknowledgment of the need for further research.
